A descriptive network analysis of the character co-appearance network in Victor Hugo's *Les Misérables* (Knuth, 1993; KONECT `moreno_lesmis`), done in R with `igraph`. It covers representations, layouts, degree distribution, centrality, clustering and cliques, global structure, community detection and assortativity.

*Coursework for Data Science Applications, MSc in Statistical Sciences, University of Bologna, by **Mohammadmahdi Ameridaragheh and Hiteshkumar Vikeshkumar Sabhani**. To reproduce it, run `rmarkdown::render("README.Rmd")`.*

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.path   = "figures/",
  dpi        = 100,
  echo       = TRUE,
  message    = FALSE,
  warning    = FALSE,
  fig.width  = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4,

)
```


# Introduction

This report presents a descriptive network analysis of the Les Misérables
character co-appearance network, taken from the KONECT repository
(`moreno_lesmis`, http://konect.cc/networks/moreno_lesmis/). Each node in the
network represents a character in Victor Hugo's novel, and an edge connects
two characters who appear together in at least one chapter. The edge weight
counts the number of chapters in which the two characters co-appear, so a
higher weight indicates a stronger association between two characters.

The analysis follows the workflow *Describe -> Visualize -> Characterize ->
Interpret*. We first describe the basic properties of the network and its
representations, then we explore its structure through visualization and
degree analysis. After that we look at node-level centrality, local
clustering, global structure, and community detection, and we close with an
assessment of assortativity and an overall interpretation.

```{r packages}
library(igraph)
library(RColorBrewer)

set.seed(1234)
```


# Defining the Network

## What the network represents

- **Nodes**: characters in *Les Misérables*.
- **Edges**: two characters share an edge if they co-appear in at least one
  chapter.
- **Edge weights**: number of chapters of co-appearance, so larger weights
  mean stronger association.

The network is **undirected** (co-appearance is symmetric) and **weighted**.

## Loading the data

```{r load-data}
file_path <- "lesmis_edges.txt"

edges <- read.table(file_path, header = FALSE, comment.char = "%",
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
colnames(edges) <- c("from", "to", "weight")

g <- graph_from_data_frame(edges, directed = FALSE)
E(g)$weight <- edges$weight
if (!is_simple(g)) g <- simplify(g, edge.attr.comb = list(weight = "sum"))
```

## Basic properties

The five lines below give the headline numbers: how many nodes and edges the
graph contains, whether it is directed, whether it is weighted, and whether
it is simple.

```{r basic-properties}
vcount(g)
ecount(g)
is_directed(g)
is_weighted(g)
is_simple(g)
```

The network has `r vcount(g)` nodes and `r ecount(g)` edges. As expected it
is undirected and weighted, and after `simplify()` it is also simple (no
self-loops or parallel edges). Co-appearance being symmetric means an
undirected representation is the natural choice. The weight attribute lets us
move beyond pure topology and account for how strong each association is.

One limitation of the data is that co-appearance in a chapter is a fairly
loose proxy for the actual relationship between two characters. Two
characters can share many chapters without really interacting, while two
others may have a single but very meaningful encounter. The network is also
limited to characters that appear in the novel, so any external context is
left out. Another small caveat is that the KONECT file labels nodes with
integer IDs rather than character names, so throughout this report we apply
the Knuth (1993) name mapping defined below.


# Network Representations

## Edge list

The first few rows of the edge list show how the network is stored
internally: each row is one edge, with its endpoints and weight.

```{r edge-list}
head(as_data_frame(g, what = "edges"))
```

## Adjacency matrix

```{r adjacency}
A <- as_adjacency_matrix(g, attr = "weight", sparse = TRUE)
dim(A)

# Sparsity: fraction of zero entries in the adjacency matrix
1 - (length(A@x) / (vcount(g)^2))
```

The adjacency matrix is `r nrow(A)` by `r ncol(A)`, and about 91% of its
entries are zero. This matches the density value we report later in the Global Structure section, since for an undirected simple graph sparsity and density add up to
roughly one.

This is the typical situation for a real-world network. The number of
possible edges in a graph grows quadratically with the number of nodes, but
the number of edges that actually form is constrained by the cost of each
connection: time, attention, narrative space, energy, money, and so on. As
networks get larger, the gap between possible edges and realised edges grows
wider, so densities shrink and sparsity grows. Social, biological and
technological networks all show this pattern.

The two representations have complementary strengths. The edge list is
compact, since it only records the edges that actually exist: in our case
that is 254 rows, compared to the 77 x 77 = 5929 cells of the dense matrix.
It is also the natural format for storing data on disk and for reading it
in. The adjacency matrix, on the other hand, makes neighbourhood queries
immediate and is the natural input for spectral methods like eigenvector
centrality. Storing it as a sparse matrix preserves these advantages without
paying the memory cost of all the empty cells.


# Visualization

We compare three different layout algorithms to see which one is most
informative.

```{r vis-prep}
deg <- degree(g)

# Character name lookup (Knuth 1993 node numbering, matches KONECT file)
char_names <- c(
  "1"="Myriel",        "2"="Napoleon",        "3"="MlleBaptistine",
  "4"="MmeMagloire",   "5"="CountessDeLo",    "6"="Geborand",
  "7"="Champtercier",  "8"="Cravatte",         "9"="Count",
  "10"="OldMan",       "11"="Valjean",         "12"="Labarre",
  "13"="Marguerite",   "14"="MmeDeR",          "15"="Isabeau",
  "16"="Gervais",      "17"="Tholomyes",       "18"="Listolier",
  "19"="Fameuil",      "20"="Blacheville",     "21"="Favourite",
  "22"="Dahlia",       "23"="Zephine",         "24"="Fantine",
  "25"="MmeThenardier","26"="Thenardier",      "27"="Cosette",
  "28"="Javert",       "29"="Fauchelevent",    "30"="Bamatabois",
  "31"="Perpetue",     "32"="Simplice",        "33"="Scaufflaire",
  "34"="Woman1",       "35"="Judge",           "36"="Champmathieu",
  "37"="Brevet",       "38"="Chenildieu",      "39"="Cochepaille",
  "40"="Pontmercy",    "41"="Boulatruelle",    "42"="Eponine",
  "43"="Anzelma",      "44"="Woman2",          "45"="MotherInnocent",
  "46"="Gribier",      "47"="Jondrette",       "48"="MmeBurgon",
  "49"="Gavroche",     "50"="Gillenormand",    "51"="Magnon",
  "52"="MlleGillenormand","53"="MmePontmercy", "54"="MlleVaubois",
  "55"="LtGillenormand","56"="Marius",         "57"="BaronessT",
  "58"="Mabeuf",       "59"="Enjolras",        "60"="Combeferre",
  "61"="Prouvaire",    "62"="Feuilly",         "63"="Courfeyrac",
  "64"="Bahorel",      "65"="Bossuet",         "66"="Joly",
  "67"="Grantaire",    "68"="MotherPlutarch",  "69"="Gueulemer",
  "70"="Babet",        "71"="Claquesous",      "72"="Montparnasse",
  "73"="Toussaint",    "74"="Child1",          "75"="Child2",
  "76"="Brujon",       "77"="MmeHucheloup"
)

V(g)$char_name <- char_names[V(g)$name]
V(g)$size      <- 3 + 1.5 * sqrt(deg)

# Label only the top 10 nodes by degree (fewer labels = less overlap)
top10_idx <- order(deg, decreasing = TRUE)[1:10]
V(g)$label <- NA
V(g)$label[top10_idx] <- V(g)$char_name[top10_idx]

V(g)$color <- colorRampPalette(brewer.pal(9, "YlOrRd"))(100)[
  as.numeric(cut(deg, 100))
]
```

```{r layout-circle, fig.cap="Circle layout.", fig.width=7, fig.height=7, out.width="100%"}
plot(g,
     layout              = layout_in_circle(g),
     main                = "Circle layout",
     vertex.label.cex    = 0.55,
     vertex.label.dist   = 1.2,
     vertex.label.degree = -pi/2,
     vertex.label.color  = "black",
     edge.color          = adjustcolor("grey60", alpha.f = 0.5))
```

```{r layout-fr, fig.cap="Fruchterman-Reingold layout.", fig.width=7, fig.height=7, out.width="100%"}
plot(g,
     layout             = layout_with_fr(g),
     main               = "Fruchterman-Reingold",
     vertex.label.cex   = 0.55,
     vertex.label.dist  = 1.0,
     vertex.label.color = "black",
     edge.width         = E(g)$weight / max(E(g)$weight) * 2,
     edge.color         = adjustcolor("grey60", alpha.f = 0.5))
```

```{r layout-kk, fig.cap="Kamada-Kawai layout.", fig.width=7, fig.height=7, out.width="100%"}
plot(g,
     layout             = layout_with_kk(g),
     main               = "Kamada-Kawai",
     vertex.label.cex   = 0.55,
     vertex.label.dist  = 1.0,
     vertex.label.color = "black",
     edge.width         = E(g)$weight / max(E(g)$weight) * 2,
     edge.color         = adjustcolor("grey60", alpha.f = 0.5))
```

In all three plots node size is proportional to degree and color encodes the
same quantity. To keep the figures readable we only label the top 10 nodes
by degree, using character names from the Knuth (1993) mapping.

The circle layout treats every node the same and forces the structure to be
read from the edges alone. The Fruchterman-Reingold layout pulls densely
connected groups together and pushes weakly connected ones apart. The
Kamada-Kawai layout uses path distances and tends to place the hubs in the
centre.

Looking at our specific plots, the Fruchterman-Reingold layout reveals the
structure best. Circle hides the community structure behind a tangle of
chords, and Kamada-Kawai compresses the periphery. Only Fruchterman-Reingold
pulls the densely connected sub-groups into visually separable clouds.

Three patterns are robust across all three layouts. First, one very large
hub (Valjean) is visibly the most connected node in every plot. Second, the
network has one connected piece: no isolated nodes drift away from the main
mass. Third, the high-degree characters cluster near each other regardless
of the algorithm. These three features are real properties of the data.

The remaining differences between the layouts are artifacts of the
algorithms. The exact angular position of a peripheral node, the overall
rotation of the layout, and the distance between two nodes that are not
directly connected all change from one plot to another and should not be
read as informative.


# Connectivity Distribution

## Summary

```{r degree-summary}
summary(deg)
```

## Distribution plots

```{r degree-hist, fig.cap="Degree distribution with frequency counts."}
h <- hist(deg, plot = FALSE)
hist(deg, col = "steelblue", border = "white",
     main = "Degree distribution", xlab = "Degree",
     ylim = c(0, max(h$counts) * 1.15))
text(h$mids, h$counts, labels = h$counts, pos = 3, cex = 0.8, col = "black")
```

```{r degree-sorted, fig.cap="Sorted degrees with top 10 characters labelled.", fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5, out.width="95%"}
sd <- sort(deg, decreasing = TRUE)
ymax <- max(sd) * 1.45

plot(sd, type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
     main = "Sorted degrees", xlab = "Rank", ylab = "Degree",
     ylim = c(0, ymax))

# Label top 10 with rotated character names
top_n      <- 10
top_names  <- char_names[names(sd)[1:top_n]]
text(x = 1:top_n, y = sd[1:top_n] + max(sd) * 0.03,
     labels = top_names,
     cex = 0.65, srt = 50, adj = c(0, 0.5), col = "black")
```

```{r degree-ccdf, fig.cap="Complementary CDF (log-log)."}
x <- sort(deg)
y <- 1 - (seq_along(x) - 1) / length(x)
plot(x, y, log = "xy", pch = 16,
     main = "CCDF (log-log)", xlab = "Degree", ylab = "P(K >= k)")
```

The distribution is clearly skewed. Most characters appear with only a small
number of others, while a few characters appear with many. The histogram
shows the frequencies directly on each bar: the lowest-degree bin contains
36 of the 77 characters, while only a single character (Valjean) reaches a
degree above 30. The sorted-degrees plot makes the same point at the level
of individual characters and identifies the top 10 by name, and the log-log
CCDF makes the heavy tail visible on a different scale. This is the typical
"few hubs, many low-degree nodes" pattern that comes up in many real-world
networks.

## Local assortativity (KNN)

```{r knn, fig.cap="Average neighbour degree vs degree."}
knn_res <- knn(g)
plot(deg, knn_res$knn, pch = 16,
     xlab = "Degree", ylab = "Mean neighbour degree", main = "KNN")
abline(lm(knn_res$knn ~ deg), col = "red")
```

The KNN plot shows the average degree of a node's neighbours against the
node's own degree. The trend line slopes downward, which means that
higher-degree characters tend to associate with lower-degree characters
rather than with other hubs. The network is therefore locally disassortative
at this level of resolution, and we will see this confirmed globally in the Assortativity section.


# Centrality

## Computing the four centralities

```{r centralities}
# igraph reads `weight` as DISTANCE in closeness/betweenness, so we invert
w_dist <- 1 / E(g)$weight

clo   <- closeness(g, weights = w_dist, normalized = TRUE)
bet   <- betweenness(g, weights = w_dist, normalized = TRUE)
eig   <- eigen_centrality(g, weights = E(g)$weight)$vector
str_v <- strength(g, weights = E(g)$weight)

cent <- data.frame(name = V(g)$name,
                   character = V(g)$char_name,
                   degree = deg, strength = str_v,
                   closeness = clo, betweenness = bet, eigenvector = eig)
```

A note on weights: in `igraph`, the `weight` edge attribute is interpreted as
a *distance* for path-based measures like closeness and betweenness, i.e. a
higher weight means a longer path. In our case higher weights mean a
*stronger* connection, so we invert them (`1 / weight`) when computing
closeness and betweenness. Eigenvector centrality and strength use the raw
weights, which is what we want.

## Distributions

```{r centrality-dist, fig.cap="Distributions of the four centrality measures.", fig.width=6.5, fig.height=5}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
hist(deg, col = "lightblue",  main = "Degree", border = "white")
hist(clo, col = "lightgreen", main = "Closeness", border = "white")
hist(bet, col = "orange",     main = "Betweenness", border = "white")
hist(eig, col = "pink",       main = "Eigenvector", border = "white")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## Top nodes by each centrality

The four tables below list the ten highest-ranked nodes for each centrality
measure, showing character names rather than raw node IDs.

```{r centrality-top}
head(cent[order(-cent$degree),      c("character", "degree")],      10)
head(cent[order(-cent$closeness),   c("character", "closeness")],   10)
head(cent[order(-cent$betweenness), c("character", "betweenness")], 10)
head(cent[order(-cent$eigenvector), c("character", "eigenvector")], 10)
```

## Agreement between rankings

```{r centrality-cor}
round(cor(cent[, c("degree","strength","closeness","betweenness","eigenvector")],
          method = "spearman"), 2)
```

The four centrality measures answer slightly different questions. Degree
counts how many direct neighbours a node has. Closeness measures how short
the average distance is from a node to all others. Betweenness counts how
often a node sits on the shortest path between two other nodes, so it
captures the role of structural bridges. Eigenvector centrality rewards
nodes that are connected to other well-connected nodes, so it captures a
sense of "influence by association".

Looking at the four tables, Valjean dominates every ranking. He is first by
degree, first by closeness, first by betweenness and first by eigenvector
centrality, which identifies him as the unambiguous main hub of the network.
Marius is second on closeness, betweenness and eigenvector centrality (and third on degree, behind Gavroche), so he acts as a secondary protagonist that shares the spotlight with Valjean.

Napoleon is interesting. He ranks third on betweenness but does not appear
in the top ten on degree at all. This pattern is the signature of a
structural broker: a character with relatively few direct connections, but
positioned on many of the shortest paths between other characters.

Cosette and Combeferre are the mirror image: they rank in the top six on eigenvector centrality but lower on betweenness. They are not bridges
themselves, but they are connected to other influential characters, which is
consistent with belonging to a tight inner circle around the main hub.

The Spearman correlation matrix supports these readings. Degree, strength,
closeness and eigenvector centrality all correlate above 0.85 with each
other, which means they largely agree on who is important. Betweenness sits
apart, correlating only 0.59 to 0.68 with the others. This confirms that
betweenness genuinely captures a different aspect of importance, while the
other three measures are largely interchangeable indicators of "hub-ness".


# Clustering and Cliques

## Global and local clustering

```{r clustering}
transitivity(g)    # global

local_clust <- transitivity(g, type = "local", isolates = "zero")
summary(local_clust)
```

```{r clust-vs-deg, fig.cap="Local clustering against degree."}
plot(deg, local_clust, pch = 16,
     xlab = "Degree", ylab = "Local clustering",
     main = "Degree vs local clustering")
lo  <- loess(local_clust ~ deg)
ord <- order(deg)
lines(deg[ord], predict(lo)[ord], col = "red")
```

The global clustering coefficient counts the fraction of connected triples
that close into triangles. Local clustering does the same calculation around
each node and tells us how tightly that node's neighbourhood is interlinked.

In our network the global clustering coefficient is around 0.50, which means
the network has many triangles and is locally cohesive. Looking at the
scatter plot, lower-degree nodes tend to sit inside small fully-connected
groups (their local clustering is close to 1), while higher-degree hubs have
lower local clustering because their neighbours don't all know each other.
This is the typical signature of a hierarchical network.

## Cliques

```{r cliques}
table(sapply(cliques(g, min = 3), length))

lc <- largest_cliques(g)
length(lc[[1]])           # size of the largest clique
char_names[V(g)$name[lc[[1]]]]   # member names of one largest clique
```

The clique-size table shows how many cliques exist for each size. There are
several hundred triangles and 4-cliques, and the number of cliques drops as
the size grows, leaving only two cliques of size ten at the top.

The largest clique we find has size `r length(largest_cliques(g)[[1]])`, and
its members are a group of characters that almost certainly correspond to a
single narrative episode in the novel, such as the group of revolutionary
students at the barricade, where many characters interact together in the
same scene.


# Global Structure

## Density

```{r density}
edge_density(g)
```

## Components

```{r components}
comp <- components(g)
comp$no              # number of components
max(comp$csize)      # size of the largest component
```

## Distances

```{r distances}
mean_distance(g, weights = w_dist)
diameter(g, weights = w_dist)
```

The density is 0.087, which is low: in a network of this size a fully
connected graph would have many more edges. The network has
`r components(g)$no` connected component covering all
`r max(components(g)$csize)` of the `r vcount(g)` nodes, so there is no
fragmentation and we can talk about distances across the whole network.

Mean distance and diameter are computed using the inverted weights, so they
correspond to weighted shortest paths. Both are small relative to the number
of nodes (mean distance around 1.1, diameter around 3.0), which is the
classic small-world signature: most pairs of characters can be connected by
a short chain of intermediaries. The network is therefore efficient and
sparse at the same time, which is the combination that defines small-world
behaviour.


# Community Detection

We use two methods so we can cross-check the results: fast-greedy modularity
optimisation and edge-betweenness (Girvan-Newman).

```{r communities}
cfg <- cluster_fast_greedy(g, weights = E(g)$weight)
ceb <- cluster_edge_betweenness(g, weights = w_dist)

length(cfg);  modularity(cfg);  sizes(cfg)
length(ceb);  modularity(ceb);  sizes(ceb)
```

## Visual comparison

```{r community-plots, fig.cap="Community partitions on the same FR layout.", fig.width=6.5, fig.height=3.2}
lay <- layout_with_fr(g)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
plot(cfg, g, layout = lay, main = "fast_greedy", vertex.label = NA)
plot(ceb, g, layout = lay, main = "edge_betweenness", vertex.label = NA)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## Agreement between the two partitions

```{r nmi}
compare(cfg, ceb, method = "nmi")
```

Fast-greedy is a fast, agglomerative method that merges nodes to maximise
modularity. Edge-betweenness is a divisive method that progressively removes
the edges most often found on shortest paths. The two algorithms follow
opposite logics, so their level of agreement (here measured by normalised
mutual information) is a useful robustness check.

In our case fast-greedy finds `r length(cfg)` communities with sizes `r paste(sort(sizes(cfg), decreasing = TRUE), collapse = ", ")`, and a modularity of Q = `r round(modularity(cfg), 3)`. Edge-betweenness finds 9 communities ranging
from `r min(sizes(ceb))` to `r max(sizes(ceb))` members, with a slightly lower modularity of Q = `r round(modularity(ceb), 3)`. Both
modularity values are well above what we would expect from a random graph,
so both partitions are meaningful.

The two methods agree at NMI = `r round(compare(cfg, ceb, method = "nmi"), 2)`, which is substantial overlap. Both
methods identify roughly the same backbone of large groups, but
edge-betweenness additionally splits some of the bigger fast-greedy
communities into smaller pieces. The largest fast-greedy community of 33
nodes broadly corresponds to the main story arc around Valjean, while the
smaller groups appear to map onto narrative sub-plots such as the
revolutionary students, the Thénardier circle, Cosette's family, and the
Bishop's group.


# Assortativity

```{r assortativity}
assortativity_degree(g)
```

Degree assortativity measures whether nodes tend to connect to other nodes
of similar degree. A positive value means high-degree nodes prefer to
connect to other high-degree nodes (typical of social networks), and a
negative value means high-degree nodes prefer to connect to low-degree
nodes (typical of technological or biological networks).

Our value is around -0.165, which is mildly negative. The network is
therefore disassortative: high-degree characters tend to connect to
low-degree ones rather than to other hubs. This matches what we already saw
in the KNN plot above. It also makes narrative sense, because
Valjean (degree 36) interacts with dozens of minor characters who appear
only briefly, rather than concentrating his interactions on a small group of
equally central figures.


# Conclusions

Coming back to the four questions the workflow asks us to answer:

**How is the network organised?**
The network is undirected, weighted, sparse and entirely contained in a
single component. It has a moderately high clustering coefficient and short
average paths, which together identify it as a small-world network with a
clear hierarchical character.

**Are there key nodes?**
Yes. The degree, strength, closeness and eigenvector centralities all point
to Valjean as the dominant hub, with Marius as the main secondary figure.
Betweenness additionally identifies Napoleon as a structural broker that
connects parts of the network even though he has relatively few direct
neighbours. The Spearman correlations confirm that the four centralities
agree on the most important nodes but disagree on the secondary ranking,
which is consistent with the different aspects of "importance" each measure
captures.

**Is it cohesive or fragmented?**
The network is cohesive overall. There is a clear giant component covering
every node, the mean distance is short, and the global clustering
coefficient is high. At the same time the community detection algorithms
identify five to nine sub-groups, so the cohesion coexists with a clear
modular structure.

**Does it show non-random structure?**
Yes. The skewed degree distribution, the high clustering coefficient, the
non-trivial modularity values and the non-zero degree assortativity are all
features that would not be expected in a random graph of the same size and
density. The communities returned by the two algorithms also map onto
narrative groupings in the novel, which gives the structure a clear
interpretation beyond the numbers.
